tierWindow.goal: Understand what exams are for and why a revision strategy matters, so that exams look like learning tools you can prepare for rather than obstacles to survive.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Recognition, recall, description and guided application (understand and identify).
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Well-defined, one idea at a time; settled distinctions such as essay versus multiple-choice exams, or revising with a strategy versus revising without one.
tierWindow.autonomy: High scaffolding; worked examples; feedback confirms and explains; frequent low-stakes checks.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: No prior experience of thinking about exams strategically is assumed. The learner is early in their studies and has met exams mainly as stressful hurdles, without a clear sense of what they are for or how preparation changes the experience; teach from first principles.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, why exams exist: what they are really for. Second, the forms exams take: the main types and what each one asks of you. Third, why a revision strategy matters: how a plan reduces anxiety and makes revision work. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about exams at university: what they are for, the forms they take, and why a revision strategy matters. By the end you will be able to explain the purpose of exams, identify the main types of exam and what each one asks of you, and say why planned revision makes a real difference.

Exams can feel like hurdles to clear and forget. They are better understood as learning tools. Seeing what they are for, and knowing that good preparation is a skill you can build, changes how you approach them and how you perform.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain the purpose of exams, identify the main types of exam, recognise why a revision strategy matters.

practiceConnection.academic: Exams run through university study. Most modules you take will be assessed by one in some form, and the way you understand and prepare for them shapes the result. Learn what exams are for and why a strategy matters now, and every exam that follows becomes something you can plan for rather than dread.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced Revising and Exams courses take you into building a full revision strategy, using active revision techniques, and performing well on exam day. Going wider: the same planning and self-awareness support Reflective Practice, Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback, and Researching and Research Methods.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Exams should look different now: not just hurdles, but learning tools with a clear purpose. You can explain what exams are for, how they support your development, give tutors a level view, and build skills such as working under pressure. You can identify the main types of exam and what each one asks of you. And you can explain why a revision strategy matters, and how a simple plan keeps anxiety in check. Look back at the confidence check to see how far you have moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, exams are something you meet in most modules of your degree. Each one is a chance to pull your learning together, and each is easier to face with a plan. The habit of asking what an exam is for, and preparing with a strategy, pays off every time you sit one, and the confidence it builds carries beyond your studies.

courseReferences.title: See pages 231 to 245 of Chapter 13, 'Revision and Exam Strategies', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
